extracted.intended_audience: academics and researchers invited to review manuscripts for journals (peer reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers serving as peer reviewers for scholarly journals, covering the end-to-end peer review workflow, reviewer responsibilities, and the different peer review models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with instructions for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal checks the paper against its instructions for authors to make sure it includes all the required sections and that it has been written in the format and style needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is part of the editorial assessment stage; failing to meet instructions can lead to rejection without further review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with journal aims and scope; originality and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor(s) check that the paper fits with the journal’s aims and scope and is sufficiently original and interesting to the journal’s audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the paper does not fit or is not sufficiently original/interesting, it may be rejected without further peer review (desk rejection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting and reproducibility checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals may carry out further checks on reporting and reproducibility at the editorial assessment stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These checks supplement editorial and peer review assessment and may influence whether a manuscript proceeds to review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum number of independent reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal will find a minimum of two independent reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invitations are sent to identified reviewers who can accept or decline; having multiple independent reviews supports editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to ethical guidelines for peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invitation is received, it is the responsibility as the reviewer to know and follow the ethical guidelines for peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should consult and comply with the journal's ethical guidelines (conflicts of interest, confidentiality, etc.) before accepting an invitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of review invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are unable to review, you must not forward the invitation to a colleague as this impacts the confidentiality for the author(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of forwarding, recommend the colleague to the editor so they can be formally invited; this preserves author confidentiality and the integrity of the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness of the review (read several times; point-by-point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers usually set time aside to read the paper several times to build a detailed point-by-point review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A careful, repeated reading supports balanced, constructive feedback; reviewers should prepare a detailed report rather than cursory comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation options in review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The review is submitted to the journal, with a recommendation to accept or reject the paper – or with a request for revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must make a clear recommendation to guide the editor (accept, reject, revise); reports are typically shared with authors alongside editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifying revisions as major or minor
rubrics_metrics.description: Revisions can either be flagged as major or minor, depending on how much work is requested to be done on the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flagging helps the editor and authors understand the extent of changes required and whether further rounds of peer review are likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor assessment of returned reviews and handling disagreements
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor considers all the returned reviews before making an overall decision. If the reviews differ widely, the editor may invite an additional reviewer to give an extra opinion before deciding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors synthesize reviewers' reports, may seek adjudication when reports conflict, and are ultimately responsible for the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicating decisions and providing reviewer reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor sends a decision to the author(s) to either: accept, reject, or request revisions. Usually, this will be accompanied by the reviewer reports – and further editorial guidance, if revisions are being requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should be transparent to authors and include actionable feedback; reviewer reports are normally shared with authors (subject to journal policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notifying reviewers of outcomes and follow-up reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: At this point, reviewers should also be told the outcome of their review. If the paper was sent back for revision, the reviewers should expect to receive a new version, unless they have opted out of further participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may be asked to re-review revised versions; for minor changes, follow-up review might be done by the editor instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article production process after acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: If the decision is to publish the paper, it will go into production and eventually appear on the journal’s website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance triggers production steps (copyediting, typesetting, online publication) handled by the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article transfer / cascade option for rejected but valid manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection may not necessarily mean the paper isn’t eventually published. Taylor & Francis offer a transfer or cascade service to some authors when their paper is rejected. If an article falls into this category, then one or more alternative journals from the same publisher will be suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can opt to submit to suggested journals (and can revise before submitting); transfer aims to find a more suitable venue within a publisher's portfolio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing reviewer reports to authors on rejection to aid development
rubrics_metrics.description: When an article is rejected, the author will receive the reviewer reports to help them develop their work further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in rejection, constructive reviewer feedback should help authors improve and potentially resubmit elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-anonymous peer review (single-blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: In single-anonymous peer review, the reviewer will know who the author of the article is, but the authors will not know the identity of the reviewers. The reviewer remains anonymous if the article is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model protects reviewer identity from authors while reviewers are aware of authors' identities; consult journal policy for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-anonymous peer review (double-blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a double-anonymous peer review, the reviewers don’t know who the author(s) of the article is. The author(s) also don’t know who the reviewers are either. The reviewer remains anonymous if the article is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both parties are anonymized to reduce bias based on identity; authors should prepare manuscripts according to double-anonymous guidelines (remove identifying information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: There are lots of different types of open peer review but typically, it means the reviewers know who the authors of the article are, and the authors will learn who the reviewers are at some point during the review or publication process. The reviewer’s name may also be disclosed alongside the article if it is published, depending on the journal policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open review increases transparency and may involve naming reviewers and/or publishing review reports; follow journal-specific open review procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: As with open peer review, this can take a few different forms. But usually, an article is published with fewer checks, then reviewers or even readers can add their own comments or reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication review allows continuing critique and commentary after publication; models vary in moderation and integration with formal records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered Reports (split peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: This process splits the peer review of a piece of research into two parts. First, the design of the study before the research is conducted, and second the paper containing the results of that work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registered Reports prioritize evaluation of study design to reduce publication bias and encourage rigorous methodology; acceptance in principle can be granted before results are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: F1000Research transparent post-publication review model
rubrics_metrics.description: F1000Research operates an innovative peer review process that is fully transparent and takes place after an article has been published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This publisher-specific model publishes articles first and then conducts transparent reviews publicly; reviewers' identities and reports may be available according to platform rules.
